item.title: Years of water shortage in Uciwai raises questions over leadership and preparedness
item.description: Families in Uciwai, Nadi, have been struggling with water shortages for years, raising questions about why it has taken the El Niño drought for action to be stepped up, despite the community having previously received water infrastructure. item.content:encoded:
Families in Uciwai, Nadi, have been struggling with water shortages for years, raising questions about why it has taken the El Niño drought for action to be stepped up, despite the community having previously received water infrastructure.

The issue was strongly raised by law student Khushboo Raj during the Fijian Media Association Town Hall Forum in Nadi, where she challenged political leaders on their responsibility to help struggling families and ensure communities have access to basic necessities.

Questioning the panel, Raj asked where is the humanity in leadership and why politicians could not use their own resources, time and personal commitment to reach out to the people who voted for them instead of depending on Government funding for every community activity.

She says elected leaders have a responsibility to represent the people, support struggling families, assist vulnerable communities and listen to senior citizens.

Using Uciwai as an example, Raj says the previous government had worked on the water tap line, but questioned why the current Government was unable to ensure even a drop of water reached the people through the piped water system.

She says families are not asking for bottled water or luxury, but need basic water to shower, cook, wash and live with dignity .

Raj also questioned why politicians spent much of their time attending consultations, media forums and meetings instead of going out into communities to see how people are living.

Raj says Fiji needs leaders who serve their communities before, during and after elections, and not only when they need votes.

Responding to the concerns, Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica says he felt part of Raj's question was a personal attack on politicians, but wanted to respond honestly.

Kamikamica says politicians do a lot of things to support people without making those contributions public.

He says he is currently supporting a family consisting of a woman and four children after the fathers of all the children deserted their wives.

Kamikamica says he supports the woman every week and does not publicise the assistance because he believes it is something that should be done as part of his responsibility as an individual.

He also reveals that someone approached him last week requesting assistance to purchase water for a settlement in Nadi, and he provided the money.

Kamikamica says he wanted to share these examples because he did not want people to assume politicians were insensitive or did not care about the country.

He says all 55 Members of Parliament care deeply about Fiji and that was why they are in Parliament.

On the specific concerns about Uciwai, Kamikamica says Nadi youth Ria Dutt had raised the same issue during the previous Town Hall meeting in Nasinu.

He says he remains in contact with her and had received an email about water issues in Labasa and Uciwai.

Kamikamica says he immediately forwarded the complaints to the Chief Executive Officer of the Water Authority of Fiji, who follows up on the issues.

He says whenever Dutt does not receive a response or the problem is not addressed, she sends him a reminder and he forwards the matter again to the WAF CEO.

Acting Manager Regional Operations Western Joeli Rabuatoka confirms that the water challenges in Uciwai have been ongoing, with WAF communicating through emails and referrals received from the community.

Rabuatoka thanks the Deputy Prime Minister for his involvement and says WAF has been supplying water to the area over the past week.

He says the authority has also been monitoring water-cut schedules to maintain the supply of water to the community.

Rabuatoka says WAF has taken further steps to verify families in the area and supply tanks to assist them during the current El Niño challenges.

He explains that Uciwai is located at the extent of the water supply system and says WAF is working on a long-term investment plan that includes upgrading the Nagado treatment plant.

Rabuatoka says the authority needs to increase production because of the growing demand in Nadi and Lautoka, and has also invested in infrastructure towards Nawaicoba.

He says WAF anticipates seeing the outcome of these investments in the next financial year.

However, when asked in why it had to take the El Niño before something was done to assist the people of Uciwai, considering it had been going on for a number of years, Rabuatoka says WAF has limited funding for water carting on an annual basis.

He says the El Niño situation has allowed the authority to access additional funding to increase water carting operations.

Rabuatoka says more trucks have been funded to assist with water deliveries to affected communities.

National Federation Party Leader Professor Biman Prasad thanks Raj for raising the concerns and says he could relate to her approach of confronting politicians, recalling that he was similar when he was a university student.

item.title: Year 11 Votualevu College student calls for return of corporal punishment in schools
item.description: A Year 11 Votualevu College student is calling for the return of corporal punishment in schools, saying it could help address student indiscipline and protect teachers, while also questioning whether Government should bring back the Year 10 external examination and strengthen the repeat policy. Sailasa Seavula raised these questions during the Fijian Media Association Town Hall Forum in Nadi at FN
item.content:encoded:
A Year 11 Votualevu College student is calling for the return of corporal punishment in schools, saying it could help address student indiscipline and protect teachers, while also questioning whether Government should bring back the Year 10 external examination and strengthen the repeat policy.

Sailasa Seavula raised these questions during the Fijian Media Association Town Hall Forum in Nadi at FNU Namaka Campus, saying education plays an important role in shaping the future of young people and that some areas need serious attention.

Seavula says examinations can encourage students to take studies seriously, prepare themselves for higher-level education and understand their academic progress.

On the repeat policy, he questions whether Government could strengthen the existing policy in secondary schools, saying some students move to the next year level without fully understanding the subjects they have been taught.

He gives the example of a student who struggles with basic English and may find it difficult to cope with Year 12, saying stronger academic support and clear standards are needed to help students improve.

Referring to a video circulating on social media showing a student damaging school facilities, he asks what Government would do to maintain the level of discipline in schools and whether it would continue issuing warnings and suspending students.

He says they have to bring back corporal punishment so students can learn how school works and do not damage school facilities.

Seavula also says teachers' boundaries are not being respected and that corporal punishment should return so students and teachers are protected.

In response, Minister for Education Aseri Radrodro says the Ministry of Education Act has expanded the Ministry's jurisdiction beyond the school environment.

Radrodro says the new Education Act 2026 empowers Ministry staff and teachers to come to students' homes, villages and communities and inquire with parents and guardians why students are not attending school or are misbehaving.

He says the new Act also covers teacher protection, including issues of bullying and student misconduct.

Radrodro says the new Education Act will be effective from 1st January, 2027.

Meanwhile, NextGen Alliance Party Deputy Leader Noeleen Billings says parents need to take greater responsibility for their children's behaviour.

She says she would like to see more parents being more responsible for their children, especially from a young age.

Billings says she would rather see parents brought into schools and asked why their children are behaving in a particular way, adding that parents should be disciplined more because they are getting away with their responsibilities.

Responding to her comments, Seavula says some students or children, after being disciplined at home, take it to the police.

Billings says children should learn manners from an early age and suggests the education system introduce more lessons on manners from Class One and Class Two.

She says it is very unfair to just blame the child because the child is doing that for a reason.

Billings also says more parents are too caught up on their phones or sitting around the grog bowl than worrying about sitting and helping their children with homework.

Drawing on her experience as a former teacher, she says she never had to punish any of her students and that it is also the way a teacher approaches a student.

S he says teachers should look into a child's background, sit with the child and spend more time asking what the problem is.

Billings says the classroom is the place to make errors and teachers are not being paid to discipline children, but to teach them the lessons they came to learn.

She says children should already know discipline before they get to school.

Liberation of Fiji Party representative Veronica Malani says there should be an integrated approach between parents, teachers and elders in society.

Malani says the Ministry of Education should conduct some psychological assessment or survey to understand the factors determining a child's behaviour, followed by consultations with parents, churches and community leaders.

She says Fiji could look at international communities that have gone through the same process and maybe amend the law so that it can at least have a bit of capital punishment.

Malani also says some students may be suffering from autism or some behavioural symptoms and says her party would pursue the proposed approach.

We Unite Fiji Party Leader Ruveni Nadalo says changes to the education system should begin from early childhood.

He says children should learn their culture and language from early childhood to Class Three, because by the time they reach Class Four, it is still intact with them.

Nadalo says children are beyond control from a very young age and that the whole education system needs to change from early childhood.

item.title: Police officer deserves a medal for disciplining students - Naivalurua
item.description: The actions of a police officer who was filmed disciplining students at the Suva Bus Stand by making them hold their ears has been defended by Minister for Policing Ioane Naivalurua, who says he would award the officer a medal for what he did, if there ever was an award for it. The video, which has been circulating on social media, has attracted mixed reactions, with some questioning whether stude
item.content:encoded:
The actions of a police officer who was filmed disciplining students at the Suva Bus Stand by making them hold their ears has been defended by Minister for Policing Ioane Naivalurua, who says he would award the officer a medal for what he did, if there ever was an award for it.

The video, which has been circulating on social media, has attracted mixed reactions, with some questioning whether students should be publicly humiliated in this manner.

Speaking to the media during the first Fiji Wastewater Drug Monitoring Report press conference at Ra Marama House, Naivalurua says there has been too much discussion on social media about the video, while greater attention should be given to the behaviour of young people and the role of parents in guiding their children.

He says Fiji is facing major issues with its young people, pointing to students roaming the streets after school.

Naivalurua says he strongly believes that the best school is at home and the best teachers are parents.

He says the behaviour displayed by the students in the video reflects what is happening in their homes, adding that parents must take responsibility for guiding their children.

On the police officer's actions, Naivalurua says he would award him a medal if one existed for what he did.

He says the incident could leave a lasting impression on the students and discourage them from repeating similar behaviour.

Using cancer as an analogy, Naivalurua says problems must be addressed in their early stages before they spread and become much bigger issues.

He says the officer's actions were, in his view, an innovative way of supporting discipline among young people and ensuring the students would remember the consequences of their behaviour.

item.title: Cannabis use highest in Lautoka, while methamphetamine highest in Suva
item.description: Cannabis remains the most commonly used illicit drug in Fiji, while methamphetamine has been detected at all four wastewater monitoring sites, highlighting the need for continued monitoring and targeted efforts to tackle drug use. Minister for Policing Ioane Naivalurua says findings from Fiji’s first Wastewater Drug Monitoring Report provide clear and reliable data on drug consumption patterns, al
item.content:encoded:
Cannabis remains the most commonly used illicit drug in Fiji, while methamphetamine has been detected at all four wastewater monitoring sites, highlighting the need for continued monitoring and targeted efforts to tackle drug use.

Minister for Policing Ioane Naivalurua says findings from Fiji’s first Wastewater Drug Monitoring Report provide clear and reliable data on drug consumption patterns, allowing authorities to better understand the extent of illicit drug use in the country.

The report found that cannabis consumption was highest in Lautoka, at approximately ten times the level of methamphetamine detected at the same site.

Methamphetamine was detected at all four monitoring sites, with Suva recording the highest level at almost five doses per day per 1,000 people, more than double the level recorded in Nadi.

Cocaine was detected only in Nadi, where its level was higher than methamphetamine, while MDMA was also found at the site but at low levels.

Heroin, fentanyl and ketamine were not detected during the first round of sampling.

Naivalurua says the findings provide authorities with reliable evidence instead of relying solely on police seizures or information reported by individuals.

He says overall illicit drug use in Fiji is lower than in Australia, however, the detection of methamphetamine across all four sites and cocaine at one site shows Fiji is not free from the regional drug trade.

Australian Ambassador to Fiji Peter Roberts says drug-related harm is a shared challenge that requires cooperation across policing, health, military and social services.

Roberts says wastewater testing, which has been used in Australia, is an important tool in identifying the scale and nature of drug consumption and helping authorities determine where resources are needed.

He says Australia remains committed to supporting Fiji through the Vuvale partnership, including cooperation with the Fiji Police Force and the Republic of Fiji Military Forces on maritime security and drug trafficking.

Meanwhile, Acting Executive Director of Mission Coordination and Analysis at the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission, Wendy Darling, says Australia recorded the consumption of 15.8 tonnes of methamphetamine and almost eight tonnes of cocaine in the year ending August 2025.

Darling says the consumption of those two drugs alone is estimated to have generated 13.8 billion Australian dollars in criminal proceeds.

She says 68 percent of illicit drug presentations to emergency departments across Australia between 2020 and December 2024 involved methylamphetamine.

Darling says Fiji's wastewater monitoring programme, strengthened legislation and regional cooperation will help the country better understand and respond to the drug threat.

The Ministry of Policing and Communications is also working with academic institutions, UNICEF and other relevant agencies to produce Fiji's first National Drug Report, drawing on wastewater monitoring, law enforcement statistics, health data and community insights.
